lessons.title: Everyday maths functions
learn: MOD, ABS, POWER, SQRT, PRODUCT, RANDBETWEEN
lessons.mac:
Recalculate now: ⌘ + =  (F9 on Windows)
Freeze random numbers: ⌘ + C, then ⌃ + ⌘ + V (Paste Special) > Values
Fill down: ⌘ + D

steps.say: Here is the finished sheet. For each salesperson we show the size of the gap from target without the minus sign, mark odd and even rows, and draw lucky numbers for a contest. On the right, a few quick calculations for an order and a plot of land.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S10-01 Done

steps.say: In this lesson you will use six small functions that come up every week at work: ABS, MOD, POWER, SQRT, PRODUCT and RANDBETWEEN. Open the practice workbook and go to sheet S10-01.

acts.t:
You will learn
• ABS for gaps without a minus sign
• MOD for odd, even and every-nth row
• POWER, SQRT, PRODUCT and RANDBETWEEN
Practice sheet: S10-01

steps.say: Here are the six functions in plain English. Each one takes just one or two arguments, so they are quick to learn.

acts.t:
ABS(number): the value without its sign
MOD(number, divisor): the remainder after dividing
POWER(number, power): a number raised to a power, same as ^
SQRT(number): the square root
PRODUCT(number1, ...): multiplies everything
RANDBETWEEN(bottom, top): a random whole number

steps.say: This is the practice sheet. Column E already has the variance, actual minus target. Priya in row 3 is short by thirty-two thousand rupees, so her variance shows a minus sign.
For a report of how big each gap is, we want the size without the sign. Click F2, type equals ABS, open bracket, E2, close bracket, and press Return.
Now copy it down. Select F2 to F13 and press Command D to fill down. Priya's gap now shows thirty-two thousand rupees, with no minus sign.

acts.h: Select F2:F13 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Next, MOD gives the remainder after division. Click G2 and type equals MOD, open bracket, A2 comma 2, close bracket. Any number divided by two leaves zero if it is even and one if it is odd.
Let us turn that into words. In G2 type equals IF, open bracket, MOD of A2 comma 2 equals zero, then comma, Even in quotes, comma, Odd in quotes, close bracket.
Fill it down with Command D. This same idea lets you band alternate rows, split work between two teams, or pick every third invoice for an audit.

acts.h: Select G2:G13 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: For a lucky draw, click H2 and type equals RANDBETWEEN, open bracket, 1000 comma 9999, close bracket. Fill it down. Each person gets a random four-digit number.

acts.h: Select H2:H13 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now the quick maths block on the right. The plot is twelve metres on each side. In K3, type equals POWER, open bracket, K2 comma 2, close bracket. Twelve squared is one hundred and forty-four.
Here is a common mistake. In K4, type equals SQRT of E3, Priya's variance. Excel shows the NUM error, because a negative number has no square root.
Point SQRT at a positive number instead. In K4 type equals SQRT of K3. The square root of one hundred and forty-four takes us back to twelve. If the sign does not matter, wrap the value in ABS first.

PRODUCT multiplies a whole range in one go. In K8 type equals PRODUCT, open bracket, K5 colon K7, close bracket. Twenty-five boxes at four hundred and eighty rupees with ten percent off comes to ten thousand, eight hundred rupees.

Everything here is live. Change the side of the plot in K2 to 15. The area becomes two hundred and twenty-five and the square root follows. The lucky numbers also change, because RANDBETWEEN picks again on every edit.
A note for Mac users. To force a recalculation and draw fresh random numbers, press Command equals. To freeze the numbers, copy them and use Paste Special, Values.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Recalculate now: ⌘ + =  (F9 on Windows)
Freeze random numbers: ⌘ + C, then ⌃ + ⌘ + V (Paste Special) > Values
Fill down: ⌘ + D

steps.say: To recap. ABS gives the size of a gap without the sign. MOD gives the remainder, which is the trick behind odd, even and every-nth row. POWER, SQRT, PRODUCT and RANDBETWEEN handle the rest.

acts.t:
Recap
• ABS(E2): the gap without a minus sign
• MOD(A2,2)=0: even rows; MOD(A2,3)=0: every third row
• POWER, SQRT, PRODUCT, RANDBETWEEN for quick maths

steps.say: Your challenge. Every third salesperson is picked for an audit. In column I, write a formula that shows the word Audit when the serial number is a multiple of three, and leaves the cell blank otherwise. The answer is on S10-01 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
In I2, show "Audit" when S.No is a multiple of 3, otherwise blank
Fill down to I13
Hint: MOD(A2,3)
Answer: S10-01 Done, column I

steps.say: Here is the finished sheet. Every salesperson has a rank, the top ten are flagged, and the panel on the right shows the best and worst figures, the ninetieth percentile and the quartiles. This is the table every sales head asks for at year end.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S10-02 Done

steps.say: In this lesson you will rank people with RANK dot EQ, pull the top and bottom values with LARGE and SMALL, and find percentiles and quartiles. Go to sheet S10-02.

acts.t:
You will learn
• RANK.EQ to rank sales
• LARGE and SMALL for top and bottom values
• PERCENTILE.INC and QUARTILE.INC
Practice sheet: S10-02

steps.say: Here is the syntax. RANK dot EQ needs the number, the full list, and an optional order. LARGE and SMALL take a list and a position, k.

acts.t:
RANK.EQ(number, ref, [order])
number: the value to rank
ref: the full list, locked with $
order: 0 or blank = largest is 1; 1 = smallest is 1

LARGE(array, k) / SMALL(array, k): the k-th largest or smallest
PERCENTILE.INC(array, k): k between 0 and 1
QUARTILE.INC(array, quart): 1 = Q1, 2 = median, 3 = Q3

steps.say: Twenty salespeople with their sales for the year. Click D2 and type equals RANK dot EQ, open bracket.
The first argument is the number to rank, C2. Then a comma.
The second argument is the whole list, C2 to C21. Close the bracket and press Return. Aarav gets his rank.
Now fill it down with Command D and look at the bottom. Farhan in row 21 shows rank 1, which is wrong. The list moved down with every row, so his formula compares him only with himself.

acts.h: Select D2:D21 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: The fix is to lock the list with dollar signs. In Excel for Mac, select the reference and press Command T. Here we type it: equals RANK dot EQ, open bracket, C2 comma, dollar C dollar 2 colon dollar C dollar 21, close bracket.
Fill down again. Now every rank is right, and Arjun with thirty-one lakh, five thousand rupees is number one.

acts.h: Select D2:D21 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now the panel on the right. In H2 type equals LARGE, open bracket, the locked list, comma 1. That is the highest sales figure.
Change only the last number for the next two. In H3, LARGE with 2 gives the second highest, and in H4, LARGE with 3 gives the third.
SMALL works the other way. In H5 type equals SMALL of the list, comma 1, for the lowest figure.
For the top ten, find the cut-off: the tenth highest. In H6, type LARGE of the list, comma 10.
Now flag the top ten. In E2 type equals IF, C2 greater than or equal to dollar H dollar 6, then Top 10 in quotes, else empty quotes. Fill it down.

acts.h: Select E2:E21 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Percentiles answer a different question. In H7 type equals PERCENTILE dot INC, open bracket, C2 colon C21, comma 0.9. Ninety percent of the team sold less than this figure.
Quartiles are the twenty-fifth and seventy-fifth percentiles. In H8 type QUARTILE dot INC of the list comma 1, and in H9 the same with 3. The middle half of the team sits between these two numbers.
Finally, the name of the top performer. In H10 type equals INDEX of the names, then MATCH of H2 in the sales column, with zero for an exact match.
Now prove it is dynamic. Change Vikram's sales in C6 to thirty-two lakh. He jumps to rank 1, joins the top ten, and his name appears as the top performer.

To recap. Rank with RANK dot EQ and always lock the list. Use LARGE and SMALL for top and bottom values, and a cut-off cell to flag the top ten. Percentiles and quartiles show where someone stands in the group.

acts.t:
Recap
• RANK.EQ(C2,$C$2:$C$21): lock the list with $ (⌘ + T)
• LARGE / SMALL with k for top and bottom values
• PERCENTILE.INC and QUARTILE.INC show position in the group

steps.say: Your challenge. In H11, show the name of the second-best salesperson using INDEX and MATCH with H3. The answer is on S10-02 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
In H11, return the name of the 2nd-highest seller
Hint: INDEX(A2:A21, MATCH(H3, C2:C21, 0))
Answer: S10-02 Done, cell H11

lessons.title: Averages and spread
learn: CORREL between ad spend and sales

steps.say: Here is the finished sheet: twelve months of ad spend, sales and leads, with a small statistics panel. It tells you the typical month, how much months swing, and whether spending more on ads actually goes with higher sales.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S10-03 Done

steps.say: You will learn the difference between average and median, find the most common value with MODE, measure spread with standard deviation and variance, and check a relationship with CORREL. Go to sheet S10-03.

acts.t:
You will learn
• AVERAGE vs MEDIAN, and MODE.SNGL
• STDEV.S and VAR.S for spread
• CORREL between ad spend and sales
Practice sheet: S10-03

steps.say: All of these take a range. The dot S versions treat your data as a sample, which is the right choice for business data. CORREL takes two ranges of the same size and returns a value from minus one to one.

acts.t:
MEDIAN(range): the middle value
MODE.SNGL(range): the most frequent value
STDEV.S(range): typical distance from the average
VAR.S(range): standard deviation squared
CORREL(range1, range2): -1 to +1; near +1 = move together
.S = sample (use this), .P = whole population

steps.say: Click G2 and type equals AVERAGE, open bracket, C2 colon C13, close bracket. The average month is about twenty-two lakh, sixty thousand rupees.

In G3 type equals MEDIAN of the same range. The median is the middle month when you sort them, about twenty-one lakh, ninety-five thousand rupees. It is a little lower, because the Diwali month of October pulls the average up.
Now the most common value. A frequent mistake is to run MODE on sales. In G4 type equals MODE dot SNGL of C2 to C13. Excel shows N/A, because no two months have exactly the same sales.
MODE makes sense for counts that repeat. Change it to D2 colon D13, the leads column. Four hundred and fifty-two leads came up three times.
Spread tells you how much months swing. In G5 type equals STDEV dot S of C2 to C13. A typical month is about six lakh, six thousand, eight hundred and twenty-five rupees away from the average.
In G6 type equals VAR dot S of the same range. Variance is the standard deviation squared, so it is in squared rupees and hard to read. We use it mainly inside other statistics.
Now the question marketing always asks. In G7 type equals CORREL, open bracket, B2 colon B13, comma, C2 colon C13, close bracket. The answer, 0.91, is close to one.
A correlation this strong means ad spend and sales rise and fall together. It does not prove the ads caused the sales. Festive months raise both, so treat it as a clue, not proof.

acts.t:
Reading CORREL
+0.7 to +1: strong, move together
-0.3 to +0.3: little relationship
-1 to -0.7: strong, move opposite
Correlation is not causation

steps.say: Here is why the median matters. Change October's sales in C8 to ninety lakh, as if one bulk order landed. The average jumps by more than four lakh, but the median does not move at all.
Press Command Z to undo. When one big order or one large salary can distort the picture, report the median alongside the average.

To recap. Report the median next to the average when outliers are possible. Use MODE for values that repeat, and standard deviation for how much things swing. CORREL shows whether two measures move together, not why.

acts.t:
Recap
• AVERAGE vs MEDIAN: outliers move only the average
• MODE.SNGL for repeating values; STDEV.S for swing
• CORREL from -1 to +1: a relationship, not a cause

steps.say: Your challenge. In G9, work out the coefficient of variation: the standard deviation divided by the average, shown as a percentage. It lets you compare swing across branches of different sizes. The answer is on S10-03 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
In G9: coefficient of variation = G5 / G2, formatted as %
Answer: S10-03 Done, cell G9

lessons.title: SUBTOTAL and AGGREGATE
lessons.mac:
Hide rows: ⌃ + 9   Unhide rows: ⌃ + ⇧ + 9
Hide columns: ⌃ + 0
Or Control-click the row headers > Hide / Unhide

steps.say: Here is the finished sheet. Some rows are hidden, and the totals at the bottom react: one total still counts everything, another counts only what you can see, and the incentive total works even though two cells show errors.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S10-04 Done

steps.say: In this lesson you will build totals that ignore hidden rows with SUBTOTAL, and totals that skip errors with AGGREGATE. Go to sheet S10-04.

acts.t:
You will learn
• SUBTOTAL 9 vs 109 with hidden and filtered rows
• AGGREGATE to ignore errors
• Hide and unhide rows with Control 9
Practice sheet: S10-04

steps.say: SUBTOTAL takes a function number and a range. Nine means sum and counts manually hidden rows; one hundred and nine means sum and skips them. Filtered-out rows are always skipped.

acts.t:
SUBTOTAL(function_num, ref1, ...)
9 = SUM, 1 = AVERAGE, 2 = COUNT, 4 = MAX
1 to 11: include rows you hide by hand
101 to 111: skip rows you hide by hand
Rows hidden by a filter are skipped by both

steps.say: Start with a plain total. Click E23, type equals SUM, open bracket, E2 colon E21, close bracket, and press Return.
In E24, type equals SUBTOTAL, open bracket, 9 comma, E2 colon E21, close bracket. Right now it matches the SUM.
In E25, the same with 109: equals SUBTOTAL, open bracket, 109 comma, E2 colon E21. All three totals agree.
Now hide the first four April invoices. Select A5 to A8 and press Control 9. Rows 5 to 8 disappear.
Look at the totals. SUM and SUBTOTAL 9 still include the hidden rows. SUBTOTAL 109 drops to thirty-one lakh, fifty-four thousand rupees, the total of what you can see.
Here is a mistake you will meet often. The incentive column has two N/A errors from a lookup that failed. In F26 type equals SUM of F2 to F21, and the total is an error too.
AGGREGATE fixes this. It takes a function number, an option for what to ignore, and the range.

acts.t:
AGGREGATE(function_num, options, ref1, ...)
function_num: 9 = SUM, 1 = AVERAGE, 4 = MAX, 14 = LARGE
options: 5 = ignore hidden rows
6 = ignore error values
7 = ignore hidden rows and errors

steps.say: In F27 type equals AGGREGATE, open bracket, 9 comma 6, comma, F2 colon F21, close bracket. Nine means sum and six means ignore errors. The total is seventy-six thousand, four hundred and thirty rupees.
A tip for filtered lists. When you filter data and click AutoSum below it, Excel writes SUBTOTAL for you, so the total always matches the rows on screen.

acts.t:
Pro tip
Filter the list (Data > Filter, or ⌘ + ⇧ + F on Mac)
AutoSum under a filtered list writes =SUBTOTAL(9, ...)
The total follows whatever the filter shows

steps.say: On a Mac, hide rows with Control 9 and unhide with Control Shift 9, the same as Windows. If the Mac uses those keys for something else, right-click the row headers and choose Hide or Unhide.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Hide rows: ⌃ + 9   Unhide rows: ⌃ + ⇧ + 9
Hide columns: ⌃ + 0
Or Control-click the row headers > Hide / Unhide

steps.say: To recap. SUBTOTAL 109 skips rows you hide by hand, and both 9 and 109 skip filtered rows. AGGREGATE can also ignore errors. Use these for totals under lists that people filter and hide.

acts.t:
Recap
• SUBTOTAL(9, ...) counts hidden rows; SUBTOTAL(109, ...) skips them
• Filtered-out rows are skipped by both
• AGGREGATE(9, 6, ...) sums while ignoring errors

steps.say: Your challenge. In F28, total the incentive for visible rows only while also ignoring the errors. Pick the right AGGREGATE option. The answer is on S10-04 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
In F28: incentive total that skips hidden rows AND errors
Hint: AGGREGATE option 7
Answer: S10-04 Done, cell F28

lessons.title: FREQUENCY and grouping numbers into bands
lessons.mac:
Microsoft 365: type in the top cell, press Return, it spills
Excel 2019 and older: select H2:H6, type the formula, press ⌘ + ⇧ + Return

steps.say: Here is the finished sheet. Twenty-five employees are grouped into salary bands with one FREQUENCY formula, and into age groups with COUNTIFS. HR uses tables like this for every compensation review.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S10-05 Done

steps.say: In this lesson you will set up band limits, count values in each band with FREQUENCY, fix a spill error, and build age groups with COUNTIFS. Go to sheet S10-05.

acts.t:
You will learn
• Band limits ("bins") for salary bands
• FREQUENCY, which spills one count per band
• COUNTIFS for age groups with from and to limits
Practice sheet: S10-05

steps.say: FREQUENCY needs the data and the upper limit of each band. Each band counts values up to and including its limit. It returns one more count than the number of limits, for everything above the last one.

acts.t:
FREQUENCY(data_array, bins_array)
data_array: the values to count (salaries)
bins_array: upper limit of each band, smallest first
Returns bins + 1 counts; the last is "above the top limit"
A value equal to a limit falls in that band

steps.say: In column F we have four limits: twenty-five thousand, fifty thousand, seventy-five thousand and one lakh rupees. Column G names the five bands, including above one lakh.
Click H2 and type equals FREQUENCY, open bracket. The data array is the salaries, D2 colon D26, then a comma.
The bins array is F2 colon F5. Close the bracket and press Return.
Instead of counts we get a SPILL error. FREQUENCY wants to fill five cells, H2 to H6, but someone left an old number in H5, so the results have nowhere to go.
Click H5 and press Delete. The formula spills straight away into all five cells. Remember: you type the formula once, in the top cell only.
Read the bands: 3, 8, 7, 4, 3. The total in H7 is twenty-five, so every employee is counted once. The person on exactly fifty thousand rupees is in the second band, because each limit is included.
Now age groups with a from and a to limit. Click L2 and type equals COUNTIFS, open bracket, dollar C dollar 2 colon dollar C dollar 26, comma, then greater than or equal to in quotes, ampersand J2.
Then the same range again, comma, less than or equal to in quotes, ampersand K2. Close the bracket and press Return.
Fill it down with Command D. Each age group now has its count. COUNTIFS is handy when you want labelled from-to bands, and FREQUENCY when you want all bands in one go.

acts.h: Select L2:L5 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: The counts are live. Amit in row 2 gets a promotion: change D2 to one lakh, twenty thousand. One count moves into the top band.
On older Mac versions of Excel, FREQUENCY had to be entered as an array formula: select all the result cells and press Command Shift Return. In Microsoft 365 it simply spills.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Microsoft 365: type in the top cell, press Return, it spills
Excel 2019 and older: select H2:H6, type the formula, press ⌘ + ⇧ + Return

steps.say: To recap. Bands need upper limits in ascending order. FREQUENCY returns one extra count for values above the last limit, and a SPILL error means something is blocking the cells below. COUNTIFS gives you labelled from-to bands.

acts.t:
Recap
• Bins = upper limits, smallest first; a value equal to a limit is included
• FREQUENCY spills bins + 1 counts; #SPILL! means cells are blocked
• COUNTIFS(range,">="&from, range,"<="&to) for labelled bands

steps.say: Your challenge. Use FREQUENCY on the ages instead. Put limits of 30, 40 and 50 in J10 to J12 and count how many employees fall in each group, including above fifty. The answer is on S10-05 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
Limits 30, 40, 50 in J10:J12
In K10: =FREQUENCY on the ages
You should get four counts
Answer: S10-05 Done, J9:K13

lessons.title: EMI and loan schedules: PMT, IPMT, PPMT
lessons.mac:
Jump to the end of data: ⌘ + ↓   (Ctrl + ↓ on Windows)
Fill down: ⌘ + D
Toggle $ in a reference: ⌘ + T   (F4 on Windows)

steps.say: Here is what we will build: a home loan calculator. Enter the loan, rate and tenure, and Excel works out the EMI, the total interest, and a month-by-month schedule showing how much of each EMI is interest and how much repays the loan.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S10-06 Done

steps.say: You will learn PMT for the EMI, IPMT and PPMT for the interest and principal parts, and how to build a full amortisation table. Go to sheet S10-06.

acts.t:
You will learn
• PMT: the monthly EMI
• IPMT and PPMT: interest and principal in any month
• A full 240-month amortisation table
Practice sheet: S10-06

steps.say: PMT needs three things: the rate per period, the number of periods, and the loan amount. A home loan rate is quoted per year, so divide it by twelve, and multiply the years by twelve.

acts.t:
PMT(rate, nper, pv, [fv], [type])
rate: interest per period = yearly rate / 12
nper: number of EMIs = years x 12
pv: the loan amount; put a minus sign to get a positive EMI
IPMT(rate, per, nper, pv): interest part of EMI number per
PPMT(rate, per, nper, pv): principal part of EMI number per

steps.say: A fifty lakh rupee loan at eight point five percent for twenty years. Click B6 and type equals PMT, open bracket, B4 divided by 12, comma. That is the monthly rate.
Next, B5 times 12 for two hundred and forty EMIs, then a comma.
Here is the common mistake. Type B3 for the loan and press Return. The EMI shows with a minus sign, because Excel treats money you pay out as negative.

The money comes in to you as a loan, so put a minus before B3. In B6 type equals PMT, open bracket, B4 slash 12, comma, B5 star 12, comma, minus B3. The EMI is forty-three thousand, three hundred and ninety-one rupees a month.

Look at B8. Over twenty years you pay about fifty-four lakh, thirteen thousand, eight hundred and seventy-nine rupees in interest, more than the loan itself. That is the number to show anyone comparing tenures.
Now the schedule. In E4, the opening balance for month one is the loan: type equals dollar B dollar 3. In F4, the EMI: equals dollar B dollar 6.
In G4, the interest part. Type equals IPMT, open bracket, the locked rate divided by 12, then D4 for the month number, the locked tenure times 12, and minus the locked loan.
In H4, PPMT with exactly the same arguments gives the principal part. Interest plus principal always adds up to the EMI.
In I4, the closing balance is the opening balance minus the principal: equals E4 minus H4. Press Return.
For month two, the opening balance is last month's closing balance. Click E5 and type equals I4.
Now fill everything down to month two hundred and forty. Select E5 to E243 and press Command D, then F4 to I243 and press Command D again.

acts.h: Select E5:E243 and fill down with ⌘ + D
Select F4:I243 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: In month one, thirty-five thousand, four hundred and seventeen rupees of the EMI is interest and only seven thousand, nine hundred and seventy-four rupees repays the loan. Jump to the bottom with Command down arrow. By month two hundred and forty the closing balance is zero.
Go back up with Command up arrow and change the rate in B4 to nine percent. The EMI rises to forty-four thousand, nine hundred and eighty-six rupees and every row of the schedule updates.
On a Mac, Command arrow jumps to the edge of the data and Command D fills down. In formulas, Command T cycles the dollar signs on a reference.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Jump to the end of data: ⌘ + ↓   (Ctrl + ↓ on Windows)
Fill down: ⌘ + D
Toggle $ in a reference: ⌘ + T   (F4 on Windows)

steps.say: To recap. PMT gives the EMI from a monthly rate, the number of months and the loan with a minus sign. IPMT and PPMT split each EMI into interest and principal. Lock the inputs with dollars so the schedule fills down.

acts.t:
Recap
• =PMT(rate/12, years*12, -loan) for the EMI
• IPMT + PPMT = EMI for any month
• Opening = last closing; closing = opening - principal

steps.say: Your challenge. For the income tax deduction on home loan interest, you need the interest paid in the first year. In B10, use CUMIPMT for months 1 to 12. The answer is on S10-06 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
In B10: total interest paid in months 1 to 12
CUMIPMT(rate, nper, pv, start_period, end_period, type)
Tip: it returns a negative number; put a minus in front
Answer: S10-06 Done, cell B10

lessons.title: FV, PV, RATE and NPER: SIP, FD and goals

steps.say: Here is the finished planner. It shows what a monthly SIP grows to, what an FD pays at maturity, how many months it takes to reach one crore, what return a goal needs, and what one crore twenty years from now is worth today.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S10-07 Done

steps.say: The four functions FV, PV, RATE and NPER all work on the same idea: money paid in regularly, growing at a rate, over a number of periods. Give Excel any three and it finds the fourth. Go to sheet S10-07.

acts.t:
You will learn
• FV: what a SIP or FD grows to
• NPER: how long to reach a goal
• RATE: the return a goal needs
• PV: today's value of a future amount
Practice sheet: S10-07

steps.say: Here are the arguments they share. Keep the rate and the periods in the same unit, and remember that money you pay in is negative.

acts.t:
FV(rate, nper, pmt, [pv], [type])
PV(rate, nper, pmt, [fv], [type])
NPER(rate, pmt, pv, [fv], [type])
RATE(nper, pmt, pv, [fv], [type])
rate and nper in the same unit: monthly SIP = yearly rate / 12, years x 12
pmt: the regular payment (negative when you pay it)
type: 1 = paid at the start of each period, as with a SIP

steps.say: A ten thousand rupee SIP at twelve percent for fifteen years. Click B5 and type equals FV, open bracket, B3 divided by 12, comma, B4 times 12, comma.
Now the payment. Type B2, then comma 0 for no starting lump sum, comma 1 because a SIP is paid at the start of each month. Close the bracket and press Return.
The answer has a minus sign. That is the most common mistake with these functions: the SIP goes out of your pocket, so Excel wants it negative.

Fix it with a minus before B2: equals FV, open bracket, B3 slash 12, comma, B4 star 12, comma, minus B2, comma 0, comma 1. The SIP grows to about fifty lakh, forty-five thousand, seven hundred and sixty rupees.
Rows six and seven show you put in eighteen lakh rupees, so the rest is growth. Now the FD. Banks compound quarterly, so in E5 type equals FV, open bracket, E3 divided by 4, comma, E4 times 4.

There is no monthly payment, so type 0, then minus E2 for the deposit. Close and press Return. Two lakh rupees becomes about two lakh, eighty-four thousand, three hundred and forty-nine rupees in five years.
Now the goal of one crore. How many months of a twenty-five thousand rupee SIP does it take? In B13 type equals NPER, open bracket, B12 divided by 12, comma, minus B11.
Then 0 for nothing saved yet, B10 for the target, and 1 for start-of-month payments. Close and press Return. It takes about one hundred and sixty-one months, a little over thirteen years.

Next, what return does a goal need? Fifteen thousand a month for twenty years, and the target is one and a half crore. In E13 type equals RATE, open bracket, E11 times 12, comma, minus E10, comma 0, comma E12, comma 1.
RATE gives a monthly rate here, so finish with times 12 and press Return. You need about 12.01 percent a year.

Last, inflation. One crore twenty years from now will not buy what one crore buys today. In B20 type equals PV, open bracket, B18, comma B19, comma 0, comma minus B17. At six percent inflation it is worth about thirty-one lakh, eighteen thousand and forty-seven rupees today.

Everything is linked. Change the SIP years in B4 from fifteen to twenty. Five more years takes the maturity value to about ninety-nine lakh, ninety-one thousand, four hundred and seventy-nine rupees. That is the power of staying invested longer.

To recap. Match the rate to the period: divide by twelve for monthly and by four for quarterly. Money you pay in is negative. FV, PV, RATE and NPER each find the missing piece when you know the other three.

acts.t:
Recap
• Monthly: rate/12 and years*12; quarterly: rate/4 and years*4
• Money you pay in is negative; type 1 for a SIP
• FV, PV, RATE, NPER: give any three, get the fourth

steps.say: Your challenge. How much monthly SIP do you need to reach one crore in fifteen years at twelve percent? Use PMT with the fv argument, in E17. The answer is on S10-07 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
In E17: monthly SIP needed for ₹1 crore in 15 years at 12%
Hint: =PMT(rate, nper, 0, -target, 1)
Answer: S10-07 Done, cell E17

lessons.title: NPV, IRR, XNPV and XIRR
lessons.mac:
Fill right: ⌘ + R   Fill down: ⌘ + D
XIRR returns #VALUE! if any date is text
Check: a real date is right-aligned and changes with a date format

steps.say: Here is the finished sheet. Two projects with the same ten lakh rupee investment are compared on NPV and IRR, and on the right, the real yearly return of a mutual fund with irregular investments, using XIRR.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S10-08 Done

steps.say: You will learn to value future cash flows with NPV, find the return with IRR, and handle real dates with XNPV and XIRR, the method used to report mutual fund returns. Go to sheet S10-08.

acts.t:
You will learn
• NPV: value today of future cash flows
• IRR: the return a project earns
• XNPV and XIRR for cash flows on real dates
Practice sheet: S10-08

steps.say: NPV discounts every value one period, so the year-zero investment stays outside and is added at the end. IRR and XIRR need at least one negative and one positive value.

acts.t:
NPV(rate, value1, ...): values from year 1 onwards
Total NPV = NPV(rate, year1:year5) + year0
IRR(values): the rate at which NPV = 0
XNPV(rate, values, dates) and XIRR(values, dates): for real dates
Investments are negative, money received is positive

steps.say: Both projects cost ten lakh rupees in year zero. A pays back faster; B pays more later. Our cost of money is ten percent, in B9. First, the common mistake: in B10 type equals NPV of B9 and B2 to B7.

This gives one lakh, sixteen thousand, one hundred and fifty-five rupees, which is too low. NPV treated the investment as if it happened a year later and discounted it too. The year-zero amount must stay outside.
In B10 type equals NPV, open bracket, dollar B dollar 9, comma, B3 colon B7, close bracket, then plus B2.

Copy it across to C10: select B10 to C10 and press Command R to fill right. Project A is worth one lakh, twenty-seven thousand, seven hundred and seventy rupees today and project B one lakh, sixty-one thousand, five hundred and two rupees. At ten percent, B creates more value.
Now IRR, the return each project earns. In B11 type equals IRR, open bracket, B2 colon B7, close bracket, and fill right to C11.
Project A earns 15.4 percent and B 14.7 percent. IRR prefers A because its money comes back sooner, while NPV prefers B. When they disagree, decide on NPV at your real cost of money.
Watch it change. Set the discount rate in B9 to fifteen percent. Now A has the higher NPV, because B's late cash is worth less when money is expensive.

Real investments do not happen on neat yearly dates. On the right are six mutual fund purchases on different days and today's value of five lakh, sixty thousand rupees. In I2 type equals XIRR, open bracket, F2 colon F8, comma.
Then the dates, E2 colon E8. Close the bracket and press Return. The fund earned about 10.9 percent a year. This is the same XIRR your mutual fund statement reports.
XNPV values the same flows at a fixed rate. In I3 type equals XNPV, open bracket, 0.08, comma F2 colon F8, comma E2 colon E8. A positive answer means the fund beat eight percent.
On a Mac, fill right is Command R and fill down is Command D. XIRR needs real dates, so if your dates are text, from a bank download for example, convert them first.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Fill right: ⌘ + R   Fill down: ⌘ + D
XIRR returns #VALUE! if any date is text
Check: a real date is right-aligned and changes with a date format

steps.say: To recap. Keep the year-zero investment outside NPV. IRR is the return; when it disagrees with NPV, go with NPV. Use XIRR and XNPV whenever cash flows have real dates.

acts.t:
Recap
• Total NPV = NPV(rate, year1:yearN) + year0
• IRR: the rate where NPV is zero
• XIRR(values, dates): yearly return for irregular dates

steps.say: Your challenge. Work out the profitability index for both projects in B12 and C12: the value of future cash divided by the investment. Anything above one is worth doing. The answer is on S10-08 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
Profitability index = (NPV - year 0) / investment
In B12: =(B10-B2)/-B2, then C12
Answer: S10-08 Done, row 12

steps.say: Here is the finished sheet. A delivery van costing eight lakh rupees is depreciated three ways over eight years, with the book value after each year, and below it a small asset register with yearly depreciation for every asset.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S10-09 Done

steps.say: You will learn straight-line depreciation with SLN, the written-down value method with DB, and the faster double-declining method with DDB, plus how to track book value. Go to sheet S10-09.

acts.t:
You will learn
• SLN: the same amount every year
• DB: a fixed percentage of the written-down value
• DDB: double-declining balance
• Book value and an asset register
Practice sheet: S10-09

steps.say: All three need the cost, the salvage value at the end, and the useful life. DB and DDB also need the year, because the charge changes every year.

acts.t:
SLN(cost, salvage, life)
DB(cost, salvage, life, period, [month])
DDB(cost, salvage, life, period, [factor])
cost: purchase price   salvage: value at the end   life: years
period: which year   month: months used in year 1 (default 12)

steps.say: The inputs are in B2 to B4: cost, salvage value and life. Click B7 and type equals SLN, open bracket, B2 comma B3 comma B4, close bracket.
Fill it down to row 14 with Command D. From year two onwards we get a DIV by zero error. This is the usual mistake: the references moved down with each row, away from the inputs.

acts.h: Select B7:B14 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Lock the inputs. In B7 type equals SLN, open bracket, dollar B dollar 2, comma, dollar B dollar 3, comma, dollar B dollar 4. On a Mac, Command T adds the dollar signs for you.
Fill down again. Every year now shows eighty-seven thousand, five hundred rupees: the cost minus salvage, spread evenly over eight years.

acts.h: Select B7:B14 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now the written-down value method. In C7 type equals DB, open bracket, the three locked inputs, then A7 for the year. Do not lock A7, so the year moves down with each row.

acts.h: Select C7:C14 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: DB charges 22.9 percent of the remaining value each year, so year one is the biggest at one lakh, eighty-three thousand, two hundred rupees and the charge falls every year.
DDB goes faster in the early years. In D7 type equals DDB with the same four arguments, and fill it down.

acts.h: Select D7:D14 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now the book value. In E7 type equals dollar B dollar 2 minus SUM of dollar B dollar 7 colon B7. Only the first B7 is locked, so the range grows as it fills down.

In F7, the same for DDB: equals dollar B dollar 2 minus SUM of dollar D dollar 7 colon D7. Then fill E7 to F14 down. Both end at the salvage value of one lakh rupees. DDB stops charging once the book value reaches salvage.

acts.h: Select E7:F14 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Now the asset register. In F18 type equals SLN of C18, D18, E18, with no dollar signs this time, because each asset has its own inputs on its own row. Fill it down to F22.

acts.h: Select F18:F22 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: The register is live. If the server rack's life is revised from six to five years, change E21 to 5 and its yearly charge goes up straight away.

One note for Indian accounts. Companies Act books can use straight line or written-down value over the useful life. The Income Tax Act uses fixed block rates on the written-down value, such as fifteen percent for most plant and machinery, which is a simple percentage, not DB.

acts.t:
India note
Companies Act (Schedule II): SLN or WDV over useful life, as here
Income Tax Act: WDV at block rates, e.g. 15% for plant and machinery
Tax WDV for a year = opening WDV x rate
Half rate if the asset is used for less than 180 days in the year of purchase

steps.say: To recap. SLN spreads the cost evenly, DB and DDB charge more in the early years. Lock the inputs with dollars, and use a growing SUM range for book value.

acts.t:
Recap
• SLN: equal charge; DB: fixed % of WDV; DDB: double-declining
• Lock inputs with $, leave the year unlocked
• Book value = cost - SUM($B$7:B7)

steps.say: Your challenge. Add a book value column for the DB method in G7 to G14, the same way as columns E and F. Check that it also ends close to one lakh rupees. The answer is on S10-09 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
In G7: book value under DB
Hint: =$B$2-SUM($C$7:C7), fill down to G14
Answer: S10-09 Done, column G

lessons.title: Project: GST invoice and sales register
learn: Amount in words and invoice numbering
lessons.mac:
Set Print Area: Page Layout > Print Area > Set Print Area
Print: ⌘ + P, then Save as PDF
Fill right: ⌘ + R   Toggle $: ⌘ + T

steps.say: Here is the finished project: a GST tax invoice that reads the buyer's GSTIN, decides on its own whether to charge CGST and SGST or IGST, numbers itself by financial year, and writes the amount in words. Below it, a sales register for the month built on the same rule.

acts.h: Go to the sheet S10-10 Done

steps.say: This project brings together LEFT, IF, XLOOKUP, TEXT, ROUND and INDEX. Every yellow cell on sheet S10-10 is yours to fill. The seller is in Maharashtra and the buyer is in Karnataka.

acts.t:
Project plan
1. Read state codes from the GSTINs
2. Intra-state or inter-state
3. Invoice number by financial year
4. Line items with CGST + SGST or IGST
5. Amount in words
6. Sales register for the month
Practice sheet: S10-10

steps.say: The rule is simple. The first two digits of a GSTIN are the state code. If the buyer is in the same state as the seller, charge half the rate as CGST and half as SGST. If not, charge the full rate as IGST.

acts.t:
GST rule of place of supply
GSTIN: 27AAGCS4821K1Z3 → first 2 digits = state code (27 = Maharashtra)
Same state: CGST = SGST = rate / 2
Different state: IGST = full rate
Rates used here: 18% and 5% (GST rates from 22-09-2025)

steps.say: Click B4 and type equals LEFT, open bracket, B3 comma 2, close bracket. The seller's state code is 27.
Do the same for the buyer. In E5 type equals LEFT of E4 comma 2. The buyer's code is 29, Karnataka.
In E6, decide the supply type. Type equals IF, open bracket, E5 equals B4, comma, Intra-state in quotes, comma, Inter-state in quotes, close bracket.
For the place of supply, look the code up in the state table on the right, columns P and Q. In E7 type equals XLOOKUP, open bracket, E5, comma, the codes P2 to P37, comma, the states Q2 to Q37.
Add a message for a wrong GSTIN: Check GSTIN in quotes. Close the bracket and press Return. It shows Karnataka. The codes are stored as text, the same as LEFT returns, so they match.

acts.h: Type "Check GSTIN") and press Return

steps.say: Now the invoice number. GST needs a unique serial for each financial year, which runs April to March. In B5 type equals, SGT slash in quotes, ampersand RIGHT of YEAR of B6, minus MONTH of B6 less than 4, comma 2.

A January date belongs to the previous financial year, so we subtract one when the month is before April. Next, ampersand a hyphen, ampersand the same expression plus 1, for the year the financial year ends.
Finish with ampersand a slash, ampersand TEXT of B7 with four zeros, so serial 42 shows as 0042. Press Return. The invoice number reads SGT slash 25 hyphen 26 slash 0042.
Now the line items. In F11, the taxable value is quantity times rate: equals D11 times E11.
In H11, the CGST. Type equals IF, open bracket, E6 equals Intra-state in quotes, comma, F11 times G11 divided by 2, comma 0, close bracket. We will check this reference in a moment.
SGST is always equal to CGST, so in I11 type equals H11. In J11, the IGST: equals IF, E6 equals Inter-state in quotes, comma, F11 times G11, comma 0.
In K11 the line total: equals F11 plus H11 plus I11 plus J11. Press Return. Then select F11 to K15 and press Command D to fill down.

acts.h: Select F11:K15 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Something is wrong. IGST shows only on the first line, and zero below it. Click J12: the formula now points to E7, not E6. The supply type cell moved down with the fill.
Lock it. In H11 retype the formula with dollar E dollar 6, and do the same in J11. On a Mac, Command T toggles the dollar signs.
Fill H11 to K15 down again. Every line now has IGST, at eighteen percent, and five percent for the solar water heater.

acts.h: Select H11:K15 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: Totals. In F16 type equals SUM of F11 to F15, copy it across to K16 with Command R, and clear G16, because adding up rates means nothing. In K18, round the grand total to the nearest rupee: equals ROUND of K16 comma 0.

The invoice total is two lakh, eighty-three thousand, four hundred and five rupees. Now the amount in words. Excel has no built-in function for Indian words, so the helper in columns M and N splits the total into crore, lakh, thousand, hundred and the rest.
Column T has the words for zero to ninety-nine. INDEX of that list with the number plus one gives its words. In B19 type equals, Rupees in quotes, ampersand TRIM, open bracket, then the crore part.
Add the lakh, thousand and hundred parts the same way. Each IF adds its part only when that number is not zero.
Finish with the last two digits, close the TRIM bracket, and add Only in quotes. Press Return. The invoice now says Rupees Two Lakh Eighty Three Thousand Four Hundred Five Only.

Now prove the rule works. Change the buyer GSTIN in E4 to a Maharashtra number starting with 27. The supply becomes intra-state, IGST drops to zero, and CGST and SGST appear at half the rate each. The total stays the same.
Put the Karnataka buyer back: type 29AAFCK7712M1Z8 in E4. Now the sales register below. In E24 type equals LEFT of D24 comma 2 for the state code.
In G24, CGST at nine percent only for Maharashtra buyers: equals IF, E24 equals dollar B dollar 4, comma, F24 times 9 percent, comma 0. Press Tab. In H24, SGST equals G24.
In I24, IGST at eighteen percent when the state is different: equals IF, E24 not equal to dollar B dollar 4, comma, F24 times 18 percent, comma 0. In J24, the total: F24 plus G24 plus H24 plus I24.

Fill E24 down to E31, then G24 to J31, with Command D. Do not include column F, or the taxable values would be overwritten. The totals in row 32 show the month's IGST of one lakh, four thousand, two hundred and thirty-eight rupees, and CGST of thirty-one thousand, five hundred and forty-five rupees, ready for your GSTR-1 summary.

acts.h: Select E24:E31 and fill down with ⌘ + D
Select G24:J31 and fill down with ⌘ + D

steps.say: A Mac note. To print or share the invoice, select A1 to K19, then go to File, Print, and choose selection, or save as PDF from the print dialog. Command P opens Print.

acts.t:
Mac corner
Set Print Area: Page Layout > Print Area > Set Print Area
Print: ⌘ + P, then Save as PDF
Fill right: ⌘ + R   Toggle $: ⌘ + T

steps.say: To recap. The first two digits of a GSTIN decide CGST plus SGST or IGST. Lock the supply-type cell before filling down. A helper split plus INDEX writes any amount in Indian words.

acts.t:
Recap
• LEFT(GSTIN,2) = state code; same state → CGST + SGST, else IGST
• Invoice number from the financial year: YEAR(date)-(MONTH(date)<4)
• Amount in words: split into crore/lakh/thousand/hundred + INDEX

steps.say: Your challenge. Below the register, in F34, count how many October invoices were inter-state, using COUNTIF on the IGST column. Then try a Delhi GSTIN on the invoice and check the place of supply. The answer is on S10-10 Done.

acts.t:
Challenge
In F34: number of inter-state invoices in the register
Hint: =COUNTIF(I24:I31,">0")
Bonus: buyer GSTIN starting 07 → place of supply should read Delhi
Answer: S10-10 Done, cell F34

checks.equals: Rupees Two Lakh Eighty Three Thousand Four Hundred Five Only
